utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please stand up? Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I would like to speak to Dr. Skavic. Good morning, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now I can see you and I can hear you. We can start our today's examination-in-chief. Let's make sure to speak slowly so that our interpreters could follow us. Let's start with your full first name and last name, the date and the place of birth, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: My name is Josip Skavic. I was born on the 26th of April, 1943, in Pakrac in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you please inform us and tell us the most important date relevant to your professional work and career?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I completed my education in Zagreb. After the school of medicine, I started working there and I'm still employed there at the institute for forensic medicine of the medical school in Zagreb. I've spent there 32 years. In the meantime, I have continued my education and I am now a specialist of forensic medicine. I am now the full time professor and the head of the department for forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please tell us what are your professional experiences relative to the identification of dead bodies, in particular relative to the victims of war. Have you ever participated in such identifications? When was that? Can you please tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: In order to be able to illustrate the answer to this question, I would like to stress the following. In the Republic of Croatia, since 1995, there have been a lot of exhumations and so far, there have -- 135 mass graves have been excavated and a large number of individual graves. 3.553 victims have been exhumed and so far, the identity has been established for 2.745 persons. The department for forensic medicine accounts for two-thirds of these cases and since I have interruptedly been involved with the work of the department, most of the identifications were carried out with my participation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Professor Skavic, in October 2000, the Defence addressed you with a request for expert testimony. Can you tell the Chamber what kind of a request that was and what was the task of the expert? What did we ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: You requested my opinion on the reliability of the identification of the dead body of Nenad Harmandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What was submitted with the request? What documents were the object of your expert testimony and opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Enclosed with the request, I received the statements of eyewitness AH, the statement of the spouse of the dead person, his son, and the opinion of Mr. Ilijas Dobraca; another expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you carried out the expertise, you submitted your findings on the 9th of November, 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. And this is the finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Professor Skavic, do you know that during the hearing of Dr. Hamzija Zujo on cross-examination your findings were used and that Dr. Zujo issued a statement with regard to your findings? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I am aware of his -- of Dr. Zujo's findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you had the opportunity to read Dr. Zujo's testimony regarding your findings?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back to your findings dating 9th of November, 2000. Your task was to say whether the identification of Nenad Harmandzic was reliable. It was carried out by Dr. Zujo. Our first question to you was whether the correct method was applied when these experts identified the body, i.e. what was your expert opinion on the method that they had applied?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: As far as the method was concerned, it was a customary, an usual method, and I did not have anything to say about the identification method.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So that is the method that you apply in your everyday practically in the same way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The second question was what was the degree of reliability of an identification carried out in such a way, carried out by Dr. Dobraca and Dr. Zujo? What was the reliability of the identification carried out by them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I already said that the way the identification was carried out is exactly the way we would do it. It is a different thing to talk about the results of such an identification. In my written findings and in my written opinion, I stressed that the results were not such as to be considered reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you notice some omissions and failures in the procedure aimed at identifying the body and in that in particular I mean the height of the body.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: In order to be able to answer this question, I must stress several elements with which I do not agree, and they are relative to the calculation of the body's height. I must also stress that in the literature, in the forensic literature, that is, there are a number of tables with factors which were used by Dr. Zujo and Dobraca. However, these tables and these factors represent the population studies carried out in some other environment, among some other peoples. Before we started identifying bodies from mass graves, we used to use similar tables authored by a French author, Rollet [phoen], because they were the closest to our population. However, they were still not sufficiently correct to represent our population. Because of that problem, when we started identifying bodies from our mass graves, we were forced to carry out a population study, which means we had to determine new factors that will be used as multiplicates -- multiplicators to measure some bones in the body so as to be able to come up with the closest approximate height of the person while the person was alive. Due to that reason, there was the difference in the factor, the factor used by Dr. Dobraca and the factor it used by me in my opinion, because the factor for the tibial bone of 3.7646 much better corresponds to our population and gives a much better result. In addition to that, I had to stress that I cannot agree with the opinion provided by Dr. Zujo according to which the difference of 10 centimetres with regard to the real height of the person while the person was alive, and the given -- and the obtained result by their calculation can be relevant. It is inadmissible to obtain the calculated, assumed height of 185 centimetres or approximately and that it is accepted as an identification element for the person who actually was 196 centimetres tall during his life.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that the calculated height excludes the possibility that the body could correspond to a body whose height was 185 centimetres during their life?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: The conclusion that it could be that person, based on that calculation, is extremely unreliable. I would like to use the opportunity and corroborate my opinion by saying that in Bosnia recently, due to this particular problem, a population study has been carried out by Dr. Sarajlic. I do not know the results of that work but I'm sure that there was a need to carry this study out for the aforementioned reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let's be more precise. Dr. Skavic, based on the data that you had from the findings obtained by Dr. Zujo and -- did you come up the same conclusions and them? If not what are the differences? What do they consist of?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: My conclusion, after I carried out some calculation was as follows: The assumed height of the person, while the person was alive, would have been around 185 to 186 centimetres, and since this differs by ten centimetres from the height of the late Harmandzic, this calculation cannot be used in a positive sense in order for the facts to be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Professor Skavic, did you see in Dr. Zujo's statement given before this Tribunal, did you see that he stated that you, in your calculation, failed to take into account the diameter of the skull and that that had a bearing on your calculation? Can you comment upon Dr. Zujo's answer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And I must say that this is yet another element which unfortunately does not corroborate and is not in favour of Dr. Zujo's opinion. Dr. Zujo said that they took into account that parameter in the following way. They express it in millimetres and then they transform it into the same value of the height in centimetres. Since that parameter was 180 millimetres, he concluded that in centimetres, it would correspond to the height of the person while the person was alive, and I don't think that one needs to provide a forensic comment to say that the height obtained in such a way would be 16 centimetres less than the height of the late Harmandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So we may say that even after this comment provided by Dr. Zujo, you continued to adhere to your findings that this has nothing to do with your findings?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: This does not have any bearing on the conclusions provided in my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let's finish with the height. What is the reliability of the identification carried out in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I must say that this was extremely unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what, in your opinion, is the reliability of the identification using clothes? One of the pathologists who testified here, testified about the identification based on clothes. What is the reliability of that identification using clothes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: When a body is being identified everywhere, the identification using clothes is extremely important. However, based on the experience we've had during our exhumations, I can say that in a number of cases, we had situations in which, before the person died, especially if that person had been taken away together with a large number of people, items of clothing would have been exchanged, swapped, so that very often the person would be identified wearing the clothes of another person. For that reason, identification using clothes is just one link in a chain of identification, and it can be used to help us come to the final identification result, but it does not represent an absolute identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What is the reliability of identification using the missile, the bullet, that was one of the elements used and testified to by one of the expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Elements such as the missile found on the body are very important. However, if the findings of the missile are correct, if we know exactly where the missile was found during the life of the deceased person and so on and so forth. However, I must stress that in this concrete case, Dr. Dobraca, in his findings, stresses the following, and I quote, "The bullet itself was found on the body of the deceased person but it was found with the body but I do not know where near the body." So in this case, we do not have the reliable data on where the bullet was found or where it was during the life of the deceased person. As a result of this, this could be just another important element in the identification, but not enough on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So in this specific case, is the identification based on objective scientific indicators or on subjective evaluation and statements of the family members? What in this case was the foundation for this identification, the objective, scientific findings or subjective factors and relative statements?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, I already said that all of these elements had to be understood only as additional means, during the identification. However, in this specific case, the identification was not carried out properly. It is insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And what in this specific case would mean a reliable scientific identification? What method would have to be used for us to be able to say that the identification was done with a high degree of reliability?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I'm going to give you some general elements. I allow that every team that carries out identifications has its own way and style of identification. It is for that very reason, and for the fact that we have huge experience in identification, I would like to give you the way that we carry out identifications. I've already said that I completely agree with the following way, the dead body to be examined, then all the bodies should be examined in order to be -- establish whether there were any anomalies or injuries during the life of the deceased person. Then the clothes should be examined by being washed, dried and examined, that all the elements which are found on the body, that is the bullet, the belt buckle and so on and so forth, but today, we are bound to take the material for DNA analysis. With regard to the modern degree of development of forensic medicine, it would be an omission on the part of the profession not to take a part of the tooth or a part of the bone for possible additional identification. In a case like this, we would certainly carry out all of these actions that I have just mentioned, and that my colleagues Dobraca and Zujo actually did carry out. But in addition to that, we would also take a sample for DNA analysis and when it would be proven that some of the elements of the identification did not correspond, and in this case it is the calculation of the height, then the DNA analysis would either confirm it or rule it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell me, is it done in mass exhumations and identifications? Is it always done? Is this method expensive to carry out when mass identifications are carried out? Is that maybe the reason why it wasn't done in this case, because it was expensive?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: DNA analysis is not done in every identification case. However, I have to emphasise that taking a sample for a possible DNA analysis, a sample of a tooth or a sample of a bone, does not cost anything, and the analysis itself is certainly much cheaper than possible speculations whether the person has been properly identified. So this method is not expensive within that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You have mentioned the family. Do you have experience which says that unreliable identifications in the eyes of the family are perceived as subjective, that these families want to find the body in order to start properly grieving? Do you have any such experiences with the families of the deceased?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: In the course of our identifications, we have indeed come across a number of cases, both positive and negative reaction of relatives. We've had families who could barely wait to get rid of the pressures of a member of the family requesting identification, so that whenever they would have the slightest hint that it could be a person, immediately accepted the identification. On the other hand, there were other people who rejected the identification in spite of a number of reliable indications that it was indeed a member of their family.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And one more question, Dr. Skavic, to conclude it. During his testimony here, Dr. Zujo when asked whether he was sure that the body had been identified as Nenad Harmandzic's body and whether it was indeed Nenad Harmandzic's body, he first said that he could not answer that question and then when additionally asked, he said that on the basis of all the details that he has received from the family, and all the indications that he has found, that he thought that the body was indeed Nenad Harmandzic's body. My question to you: Would that be a common response of an expert witness or would it relate only to this specific case? That is what is the expert called upon to do? Does he need to be very accurate or can he do it in that manner?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: When I read Dr. Zujo's report, I indeed found his opinion about the reliability of Harmandzic's identification. In his report he says in one place that he is sure, in another place that he is not sure. I cannot comment on the opinions of other experts. All I can say is that neither I nor any colleague who performed -- who performed such an identification in our institution would say that the identification was complete. However, there was something else which surprised me in Dr. Zujo's report, because when I read it, I came across an answer we shall now quote, and which says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately the interpreters do not have the text of the report.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: "Yesterday I said that a medical expert witness completes his task at the moment of the beginning of identification so that today, there was no need to take DNA analysis for the sample." And in this respect, I can only think of two possibilities: Either Dr. Zujo was confused or somebody misinterpreted his response, because the medical expert's witness is not over until the completion of identification and I do not know whether he truly thinks that the work of the forensic pathologist stops, because I don't know who else then conducts the whole procedure, the whole identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Skavic, thank you very much. Those are my questions to you and now you'll be asked some questions by my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, my name is Douglas Stringer. I'm an attorney for the Prosecution. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, it's my understanding this is not the first time you've given evidence in proceedings here at the Tribunal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You testified, sir, as an expert witness in the same field on behalf of the Defence some years ago in the Kupreskic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in fact, your testimony in that case was led by my learned friend, Mr. Par, who is a member of the Defence bench in this case. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you travel to the Hague to give your testimony in that case, the Kupreskic case?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I travelled to The Hague and I testified there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, do you speak English or understand English?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I do not speak it but I can understand it up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, just a few preliminary questions about your opinion letter, the one that's dated from November of 2001. Dr. Skavic, your opinions, your conclusions that is you've given in this case, I understand, sir, that those are based on materials that were provided you -- to you by Defence counsel, such as witness statements of various persons whom you've referred to in your direct examination. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I have just one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in addition to those materials that were provided to you by counsel for Mr. Martinovic, sir, then you I guess more recently reviewed the testimony of Dr. Zujo from this trial?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I familiarised myself with the opinion of Dr. Zujo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the testimony of any other person who is appeared as witnesses in this trial here in The Hague, prior to today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: No. The information, the facts that I had at my disposal are quoted in my answer to the introductory question by Mr. Par, and that is an eye -- in the statements of the eyewitness and the wife of the victim and the opinion of the expert witness, Dobraca and the testimony of Dr. Zujo. As for other witnesses, I never heard them, nor do I know what they testified about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that there may well be data before the Trial Chamber in this case concerning the identification of Mr. Harmandzic that you're not aware of?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I have pointed out that I did my analysis only on the basis of the facts that I quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that therefore, sir, your conclusions could well be affected by the presence of additional data that you're not aware of. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that, sir, would you agree with me that ultimately it's for the Trial Chamber to decide the weight or the credibility that it will assign to the identification based on all the evidence before it in this trial?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't agree more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness be shown Exhibit P113.2. Dr. Skavic a moment ago I asked you if you spoke or understood English. It's because I have a letter here that's been published -- excuse me, an article that's been published by you and others, some of your fellow colleagues in 1992. I have an English-language version of it. We do not have the Croatian-language version. Has that article been placed in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is an article from the Croatian medical journal entitled "identification of the dead in war. The case of the 20 killed Croatian soldiers found near Pakrac." My question, sir, is: Did you co-author this article together with other colleagues at the department of forensic medicine in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with the assistance of the interpreters, Dr. Skavic, I'd just like to ask you very few questions about some of the things that are contained in this article pertaining to the general methods used in identifying victims of war. First of all, sir, this is an article that contained your findings, your expertise, based on examinations of 20 Croatian soldiers who had been captured, tortured and killed, by Serb forces during the early stages of the war in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And turning to the second page of this article, what you've done is to provide or identify two protocols that you formulated in the process of identifying the remains of such persons, and I can just continue on. Protocol A, as you indicated, would refer to data that's would collected by members or relatives of the deceased person. It's a generalisation but is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then Protocol B would have included the data gained during the autopsy examination itself. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And among the criteria obtained or the data obtained from family members, we include a number of the same factors which have been discussed in this particular case, including age, height, belts, shoes, et cetera. Are those among the criteria that you would consider, the data considered in determining or trying to determine the identity of a given cadaver?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then there is also in both Protocols A and B a heading for miscellaneous data. Would we be correct perhaps in this case to put the presence of the 6.35 millimetre bullet that was found, could we put that in the miscellaneous category?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could do that, but once again, emphasise the importance of that particular element.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, in your direct, you already answered my first question on this point, which was to simply put to you that in fact the methodology used by doctors Dobraca and Zujo in this particular case seem to be very similar, if not identical to the methods or the methodology that you employ as indicated in your article here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I have pointed out already, yes, that the approach was identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My second question, sir, is that it appears to me that in these two protocols, no single factor is given particular weight. They are not graded or weighted, which would suggest to me that simply the identification, if it can be made, is based upon consideration of all the factors collectively. Would you agree with me on that point?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in fact, and I'm looking at the second column on this same page, about two-thirds of the way down, you indicated that in respect of these 20 Croatian soldiers, well, in fact, you and your team were able to identify 19 out of those 20 soldiers. Do you recall whether that's correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly but it transpires from the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the text on one point of the text I'm interested in reads: "Ten cadavers were identified on the basis of two or more positive findings, and nine on the basis of only one positive finding. Considering the extensive post-mortal changes of the cadavers, the high number of identifications on the basis of two or more findings is surprising."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I do not understand why is it surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My question, sir, is the fact that you were able to identify nine of these soldiers on the basis of only one positive finding. Does that indicate that a -- one of the factors or one of the protocols indicated could itself give rise to a positive identification?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: As it transpires from the text, it is indisputable and of course I'd like to refresh my memory. Of course going through each and every of these protocols to see which was the particular element which led to the identification of a particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ultimately, Dr. Skavic, it's a matter of judgement based on consideration of all the factors. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Skavic, I'd like to turn now from your article and discussion of the general methodology used, to a discussion of some of the factors that are present here in respect of the body of Mr. Harmandzic and the identification of that body. And again, continuing on with your method or the protocol that you've identified, would you agree with me, sir, that we do have good, solid match between family information and autopsy information in respect of a number of factors?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite, information from -- received from the family is fundamental important, and in this particular case, relatively precise. On the other hand, I have already pointed out that one of the chief elements, and that is the height, was -- had not been confirmed by the -- during the identification. Quite to the contrary. It is highly dubious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I understand that's your testimony, Dr. Skavic, and I'm going to ask you about the height issue in a few moments. First I'd like to talk about some of the non-height factors so that we can get those out of the way. You have not challenged the finding of Dr. Zujo, that the age of this body was approximately 45 years old. Is that a determination that can be made fairly accurately and consistently by persons in your field?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: The approximate age of an individual can be established on the basis of a series of different elements and I'd like to seize this opportunity to say that the team engaged in identification, and I points out once again that in our view, needs, in addition to a forensic expert, include a stomatologist and an anthropologist and the team because the anthropologist is called upon or I should say perhaps he is the most qualified person to establish the age of an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to challenge the finding that this was a cadaver approximately 45 years of age, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that in fact, Mr. Harmandzic was born in 1947, which would have put him at approximately 46 years of age in July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall whether I knew that or not, but obviously, since it was not important for my part of the report, I did not even -- I didn't comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then passing on to some of the articles of clothing, you're aware, sir, that there is information, or there is evidence that family members identified a shoe or a moccasin found with the body of the cadaver and that it matched approximately, quite closely, in fact, the known shoe size of Mr. Harmandzic when he was living?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that, that the footwear was like the footwear that the late person wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, sir, if there is testimony before the Trial Chamber in this case concerning the clothing worn by Mr. Harmandzic shortly before he was last seen in July of 1993, that is not something that you have considered as part of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did include it, of course, and I also emphasised that this element, in itself, does not suffice for an identification.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are sorry but they are beginning to lose the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this part of the question, because the witness is being confronted with certain things which I do not think are quite accurate, namely during the presentation of our case, we had several testimonies, several witnesses, whom we asked what had Harmandzic worn, and we received different answers, and I therefore think that it would not be fair on this expert witness to suggest that we allegedly have it established beyond any doubt what he looked like and what he wore a day before that, because it is simply not true. We have some different testimonies. Let me remind my learned friend that one said that the last time he was seen, it was in white shorts and so on and so forth, a pair of jeans was found. Therefore, I object to this form of leading the witness, of insinuating to the witness to certain things which are allegedly beyond question when, in point of fact, they are under a serious question mark. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that all the factors concerning the identification should be taken into consideration, and the Prosecutor is entitled to ask some questions about some other facts other than the height. Let us hear what the witness is going to tell us, because we lose him, part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think what I'll do actually is to ask the question in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, it's my understanding that your main point in respect of the clothing worn is that you found a number of cases in your own experience where clothing had been changed or exchanged in these wartime conditions so that that casts some doubt on the use of clothing as an identification tool. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: In answer to this question, I wish to point out that the clothes per se do not suffice for identification, especially if we are dealing with such an article of clothing which is -- which is worn by a large number of people in a particular population. There is no need for me to emphasise that a large number of people sport jeans, and that therefore one could hardly identify a person by that particular article.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Again, sir, it's just one of all of the factors to be considered, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Several other items were found with this cadaver, Dr. Skavic, one being an elongated cigarette lighter and also a belt buckle identified, as you know, by the son. Aren't these two factors which are rather persuasive, strongly suggesting that, in fact, the cadaver is that of Mr. Harmandzic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, and I emphasised the correctness of these elements. I must add to that based on these elements, there is a doubt that the body examined was the body of the late Mr. Harmandzic. Unfortunately, I have to say something else. All of these elements are not enough for a certain identification, due to the lack of elements for the establishment of the height of the person while the person was living.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And as I said we are going to come to height in a minute. So at this point, Dr. Skavic, we've discussed age, of course there is no dispute that this is the cadaver was a male and Mr. Harmandzic was a male. Identification of shoe size. Shoe. Cigarette lighter, belt buckle, blue jeans. At this point, sir, you're still not satisfied that a positive identification could be made?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: If we excluded the height that you said you wanted to talk about later, all of these elements suggest that the cadaver belonged to the late Mr. Harmandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then now just a few questions about the 6.35 millimetre bullet. In your opinion letter, Dr. Skavic, you said that -- and I'll quote: "It would be an identification element of a really great significance had that projectile been found in the soft tissues around the femur." Do you recall writing that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was seized of the data that Harmandzic, during his life, allegedly had a penetration wound in the upper leg, and that the projectile remained in the tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Skavic, are you aware that in respect of this particular cadaver, because of the way it was buried and the length of time it spent, it was in the ground, there was really no soft tissue? You've read Dr. Zujo's testimony on that point, have you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. However, this does not change my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, sir, it would have been impossible for the bullet to be found in the soft tissues around the femur, as you say, because in fact there were no soft tissues remaining, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely true. However, as a forensic expert, cannot claim that the projectile had ever been in the soft tissue because of the fact that there was no soft tissue. I can only rely on Dr. Dobraca's information who had found the projectile but he doesn't know where he found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Skavic, is it your testimony, sir, that in cases such as this, where there is no remaining soft tissue, the presence of a bullet, with the cadaver, is of no consequence? Is that your testimony? Is means nothing to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I already said that it is a very important element, but if a bullet is found somewhere with the body, we cannot claim that it used to be in somebody's upper leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in this particular case, sir, is it impossible to make that determination?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: We cannot claim that it was in the upper leg. With regard to the circumstances of this case, we can assume that this is really the case, that this bullet once was in the upper leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Knowing, having learned from the family that in fact, Mr. Harmandzic did suffer a self-inflicted wound while handling a handgun, a wound to the leg, would you agree with me, sir, that the finding of this bullet is significant but that it is not of -- it would have been of greater significance had we known precisely where it was found?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So again just to -- I want to try to summarise where we are to this point, Dr. Skavic. We now have the presence of this bullet. We know that Mr. Harmandzic had shot himself in the leg some years earlier. Together with all of the other factors, identification of the shoe by the family, correct shoe size, belt buckle, cigarette lighter, clothing, age. Are you still -- let me ask you the question this way, Dr. Skavic: Based on all of those factors, disregarding height for now, based on all those factors, do you exclude the possibility that the cadaver was in fact that of Nenad Harmandzic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I have already pointed out that these are elements that would suggest that this was indeed the person in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, you've testified about your extensive experience in your own home country of Croatia, examining the remains of persons who lost their lives during the conflict there. I'm going to ask the Registrar to show you two exhibits, Exhibit 802.13 and 802.14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, while the Registrar is doing that shouldn't we point out to Dr. Skavic, and I take on board what he says as an expert, that in fact the identification of the shoe goes further than the shoe size but in fact [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, what you just heard was a statement by our Judge Clark, and I wanted to -- I should then ask you, are you aware that in addition to the size of the shoe, this moccasin that in fact it was positively identified as being one of Mr. Harmandzic's shoes, that it was recognised by its colour and style, what have you? If a family member were to make such a positive identification, would that also be a factor, together with all the others, strongly suggesting the identification of this person?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were provided with the statement of [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, do you have Exhibit P802.13 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What you have, sir, are three pages, the top page is an English translation and under that is a two-page document which I believe bears your signature. Does this in fact bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: These are findings of an autopsy and identification procedure which you conducted in October of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you wish to take a moment to look it over, I'm going to direct your attention to the last section, which is the opinion. Sir, these are public proceedings. I'm not going to mention the name of the person who is referred to in this record, but would you agree with me, sir, that a positive identification was made and approved by you in this particular case based on the finding of a pocket watch with a particular drawing or inscription on it, consideration of the pre-death height, clothing, folding knife and teeth and the fact that, in fact, the son had identified the deceased person?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I would have to explain how this was done. This arises from the elements stated in the opinion. In addition to the forensic part of the examination of the cadaver and the clothing, the assumed pre-death height matched the information obtained from the family. The condition of the teeth is always examined by a dentist, who compares the denture of the cadaver with the denture of the same person while the person was alive. In addition to that, there were other elements, the pocket knife with the locomotive and the knife, and after that, the son recognised his father. So it was not the son who gave and recognised the identification elements, but they were first established by pathological and forensic examination and then subsequently confirmed by the son. I can say that none of the elements were contrary to the elements given by the son, because if there was no match, the identification would have been dubious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on the basis then of the information before you, it was -- you felt sufficiently confident that the cadaver was in facts the body or the remains of the person whose name appears on this record; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Not based only on information but based on the confirmation obtained by forensic examination, based on the dental status which was established by a dentist and based on the information obtained from the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, now, this record doesn't make reference to any independent dental findings. So I'm a bit curious as to how you're aware of independent dental findings when they are not referred to in your opinion. Can you shed some light on that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you how we work at my department. Whenever an identification is carried out, all the elements are stored, the complete denture is taken out when the bones are cleaned, the denture is examined by a dentist who compares it with the records of the person while the person was alive. What you have in front of you are just the elements based on which the identification was established, because that is the way we were required to draft the findings. All the other elements are stored in the department, and these elements are the dental status, the findings of the dentist, pre-mortem data given by the family, the samples of the clothing, and everything else that exists. This is all documented by photos which are all filed. So what you have in front of you are just some of the elements, those based on which the identification was carried out, not the entire case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will take a 30-minutes break. We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer. Please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps if I put on my headphones, I can hear you. Dr. Skavic, coming back to Exhibit 802.13, just one or two final questions to sum up on your last comments. The opinion on the identification of this particular person makes no reference to any dental examination or records; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: In my last answer, I said that what you have in front of you is just an opinion from which the identification elements stem, and I also explained the procedures which this is based on, and I also said that in addition to a forensic pathologist, if the important has a denture, then a dentist has to participate in the examination. Everything else is recorded by photos by the findings of experts, and this is just a group of elements based on which we assume that this was the person in question and in this particular case, the son recognised his father based on all these elements. In here, you won't find anything else but these elements. Everything else is archived in our department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Am I correct to assume, Dr. Skavic, that you don't have any personal recollection of this particular autopsy? You don't have any recollection whether, in fact, this person had any dental records?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: It is impossible for me to remember. I am just talking about the way this is done. And what I am saying is that you cannot expect to find in this document anything else but the elements based on which the positive identification was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Passing, then, to the next exhibit, Dr. Skavic, 802.14, it bears the same date, it appears that this one also bears your signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again without mentioning the name of the cadaver or the family member making the identification, this report contains your opinion of a positive identification based upon the data referred to in that opinion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, based on these last two reports that we've looked at, sir, I want to suggest to you that in fact you've been quite -- you certainly seem confident enough in these two cases to make positive identifications based upon significantly less data than we have in the case of Mr. Harmandzic. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't. In order for me to explain this conclusion, I must say that some identification elements bear more significance than others. Let's not get embroiled in some theoretical considerations. Let me just explain this on the example of the cadaver of Mr. Harmandzic. Here we have two groups of elements. You will allow me at this moment to exclude the bullet from the consideration, because the pathologist did not know where the bullet was found. There are two groups of elements. One of which contains the shoe, the buckle, the lighter and the blue jeans. We will all agree that these are the elements which can be found on a person, next to the person, or on some other person. In distinction to this first group of elements, which do suggest that the body belonged to Mr. Harmandzic, there is another group of elements which are based on what is indivisible from the dead body and those are the bones. On the one hand, we have the elements that suggest something, and on the other hand we have an element which excludes something, and that second element is of much more significance than the first elements, and to sum up, I would like to say that that second element imposes another verification. So these are the two groups of elements. When you compare the identification which was carried out at the department of pathology with the identification of Harmandzic, in Harmandzic's case, the dental status was not established, and here we do have dental status. Here, the height was measured and it corresponded to the living person in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, it seems to me that really for you the decisive, the critical point, in all of this is the calculation of height and whether that reconciles or not to the estimation of height given by a family member. Is that the crux of your conclusion in respect of this matter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just one last question in respect of these other autopsy reports that we just looked at, P802.14 and 13. No indication, sir, in any of these or either of these of any DNA sampling. Is that because a positive identification was made?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: The DNA analysis are done only when other conventional methods of identification are not fully reliable. In every other case, it is not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In your judgement, sir, it was not necessary to do DNA it testing in respect of these two other cadavers? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Skavic, we are going to now move on to the next -- the final issue, actually, which is the discussion of the height calculation. And just to, I guess summarise or review, it's my understanding, sir, that your calculation, your conclusions on this, are arrived at in the following way. Accepting that the length of the femur was 50 centimetres, Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 14898 to 14907. you applied a multiplier of 3.76, giving rise to an estimated height of living of 188 centimetres. Is that correct? I'll continue to the next point, which is the humerus bone. But for the femur, is that what you did? 50 centimetres times 3.76?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you also factored in the length of the humerus, which is the upper arm bone which was 36 centimetres, multiplied by 5.06, giving the product as 182.16 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you took the average of those two numbers, arriving at a final estimation of 185.08 centimetres as the assumed, living height of the cadaver.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Dr. Zujo appears to have used a little bit of a different method. It's my understanding, sir, and I've reviewed his testimony, as have you, that he took the 50 centimetre length of the femur, used a multiplier of 3.66, arriving at a figure of 182 to 183 centimetres, to which he then adds five centimetres to arrive at the assumed living height of the cadaver, which would have put him at approximately 187 to 188 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: As regards this part, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I understand your testimony, sir, that he used tables that differed from those you would have employed, and that may account in some respect for the difference in the initial figure of 182 that he arrived at. I'm not going to ask you about which tables are the right ones to use. My question is this: Whichever which one does the calculation, sir, it appears to me that somehow you and Dr. Zujo arrived at essentially the same conclusion. He's in the range of 187 to 188, you're in the range of 185. Dr. Zujo mentions a margin of error of plus or minus two centimetres. It would seem to me, sir, that you and Dr. Zujo are not significantly apart in your two calculations. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: You are if you take only this particular factor into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And maybe I'm anticipating what you're thinking. The problem that you have, sir, is not so much with Dr. Zujo's conclusions, your problem is with the estimation of height given by the family member, 196. Is that for you the decisive element?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Now it is necessary to mention another aspect which I did not cover in my report and which doctor Zujo held against me. According to him, in view of the skull diameter, it turns out that that particular skeleton, that is the one that the skull belonged to, was 180 centimetres high. So Dr. Zujo has the elements to calculate the height, which vary from 180 to 190 or perhaps a couple of centimetres more. This is not a way to calculate somebody's weight -- height, excuse me. Regardless of the range that is the variance from 16 to five or six centimetres, it simply can not be accepted as the final identification element, and all it comes down to is that I say that such identification should be subjected to a reliable test.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It I believe was your testimony on direct, Dr. Skavic that you reject the use of the cranium diameter measurement as a way to determine height; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I merely point out that Dr. Zujo accepts that criterion and uses it to make his identification, and I cannot agree with the final result that he obtained in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm trying to focus, then, on one of the criteria which both of you used which is femur length and again just the final point on that, sir, it appears to me that whatever methods were used, you and Dr. Zujo arrive at essentially the same place when doing your calculation based on femur length. Would you agree with me on that point?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: About 185 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, now, actually, on femur length alone, you arrive at 188, and then that number is reduced by the inclusion of the calculation based on humerus; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not hear the end of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic could you repeat the last part of your answer, please? We weren't able to get it in English.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I calculated the femur length and got 188 centimetres. Humerus, 182.16, and as the mean value, 185.08 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I understand your testimony, sir, then, it's your position that neither your figure nor the figure of Dr. Zujo can be reconciled to the estimate of height given by the family member, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The margin of error, sir, Dr. Zujo speaks of a margin of error of plus or minus two centimetres. Do you recall that testimony? It's also in his expert report.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: You're right, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo went on to testify that, in fact, others might use a greater margin of error, up to perhaps as much as ten centimetres, plus or minus. Did you read that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, what margin of error do you employ in making your calculations of height based on the length of long bones?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I have already answered a similar question, to -- and explained that before we started the identification, and precisely because of the problem involving factors and tables, applying to some other populations, not to our population, and because of that, we conducted a population study, which means that we took a large number of cadavers, and measured the length of the bones to determine the average factor which holds for our population in calculations of this kind. So when one measures the length of a femur, multiplying by our multiplier, by our factor, that is when we get, as a rule, always an approximately identical length of the body in lifetime, but can be at variance for not more than two or three centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Two or three centimetres so in fact the margin of error that you would accept is greater than that used by Dr. Zujo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, it seems to me that Mr. Stringer did not hear well what Mr. Skavic said. We heard one or two centimetres. So could Mr. Skavic perhaps repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let us make sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Zujo, we may have had a problem with the interpretation or we may have misunderstood what you say. What was the margin of error that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned one to two centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you accept, sir, that qualified experts in your field would utilise greater margins of error than one to two centimetres?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact presented by Dr. Zujo, to accept that the identification, even if the difference is ten centimetres, I cannot agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat the question. With respect, I don't think you answered it. Would qualified experts -- could qualified experts in your field use different margins of error, greater margins of error, than your own?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What margin of error do you assign to the estimate of height given by the family member in this case? Do you give him any margin of error whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: The information supplied by the family cannot be commented on my part because that is their impression. Something subjective, that I cannot influence in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it your experience that family members can be mistaken in estimating the height of a particular family member, given that it is a subjective -- can be a subjective estimation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is Exhibit P956 -- yeah, P956. It's the last exhibit. Dr. Skavic, this exhibit is an article that I found published in the American Journal of Physical Anthropology, in the year 2000. I have only two questions about it. I'm going to direct your attention to the third page, which I will read just a few sentences to you. I want to ask your opinion on something that's been stated in here. The bottom, the last paragraph of page 3. "The results obtained with the femur are better than the results obtained with the humerus, that is the coefficients of regression and the standard deviations are better. And consequently, the confidence intervals for the femur are lesser. In this connection, when we have both bones to be measured, it is not important to measure the humerus. Measures the femur will suffice and the height can be calculated from this measurement because the results thus obtained will be the best." Dr. Skavic, do you agree with that assertion that femur length alone can give rise to a more accurate calculation of height than if one were to do what you did, which is to also factor in length of humerus?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I cannot comment on this paper right now because I haven't read it. However, I can say that we also accord priority to the femur length, and if there are two bones, then the length of the cadaver and the assumed lifetime height are based on the femur and the tibia length, never on the basis of the humerus.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphones? Because we are beginning to lose the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic we got your last answer. The interpreters are asking to you move a little closer to the microphone so that they can hear you better. Okay. And then just to review the mathematics here, Dr. Skavic, relying on the femur length alone, then, that would give us a calculation of approximately 188 centimetres if one uses the multiplier of 3.76 that you used?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the only other question I wanted to ask you about this article is if you turn another one, two, three, four, five, turn another five pages of this same document, P956, what we find are what are called regression formula. This is on the page immediately following the page with the photographs of the two femurs. Do you have that, Dr. Skavic, a page containing --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, just skipping down past the formulas for females to the formulas for males, it appears to me, sir, that this author of this article has in fact used margins of error, or what he calls "confidence intervals," of nearly 7 centimetres, 6.90 or 6.96 depending on whether the measurement of the femur is the physiological or the perpendicular length. Sir, would you accept that qualified experts in your field may in fact use margins much error or so-called "confidence intervals" of up to seven centimetres?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: As I have already stated, it is a paper that I'm not familiar with, so I do not know what the authors did, what kind of material they used, in which way they worked, and therefore, I cannot comment on this at all. I have to go back to the identification method that we apply, and emphasise factors and the expected margin of error. Therefore, in our work, and in view of our factors, we never accept an error of plus-minus seven centimetres. If we were faced with such an error, then that identification could not be positive and we repeat once again, it needs to be confirmed or again refuted by more reliable method, because if somebody allows an error of plus-minus seven centimetres, that means a foot in centimetre height, from the smallest to the -- to the biggest possible, as resulting from such calculation. And this is not a way to consider an identification as absolutely objectively proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Dr. Skavic, you're not aware of any published literature in which experts in your field have used margins of error of greater than one or two centimetres? You'd reject any margin of error greater than two centimetres? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I was talking about the methods we used for identification, and I said that unfortunately, we do have experience with the number of identifications, out of all the exhumed persons so far, in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, we have come up with 81.9 per cent of positive identifications, which is an extraordinary result. Therefore, as far as I my work is concerned, our factors, that we used in order to obtain these results, are the most competent ones. Whether somebody else does differently, allows a different margin of error, and how much, for the time being, for my estimates and for my identification methods, is not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me put the question to you this way, sir. Would you agree with me, sir, that a fully qualified expert in your field may in fact use a margin of error of up to seven centimetres or six centimetres as opposed to the smaller margins of error used by you and your staff? Could a different expert, fully qualified, justifiably important a greater margin of error?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: In the specific case, Dr. Zujo, is an absolute expert. If he says that he tolerates a larger errors, that is up to him. He is responsibility for his work. I am responsible for my work, and I would never say that this case is the case of a positive identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in addition to Dr. Zujo, sir, it would appear that the author of this article that we have been referring to would also tolerate a margin of error of up to nearly seven centimetres. Would you agree with me on that point?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I don't know what the author or the authors of this paper did, and if I am asked to answer this question, I would need sometime to study this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, if you had performed a calculation the way that's indicated, at least by the author of this article, relying on femur alone, applying your multiplier of 3.76, and then utilising a margin of error of plus or minus seven centimetres, isn't it true, sir, that you would arrive squarely within the range or you could arrive at a conclusion that is consistent and reconcilable with the estimate of height given by the family member in this case, of 196 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object. My learned friend is quoting a paper and then speculates what would happen "if." Professor Skavic told you clearly that he couldn't comment on this paper, because he hasn't read it. There is no translation. He hasn't read it. And now he is being asked to speculate what would happen if he did or if he used something that he didn't use. If my learned friend insists, then I believe that Professor Skavic should be enabled to read this paper so as to know what he is supposed to talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, I think your question is very obvious, which is that every lay plan could do his own calculation according to this formula. There is no need to put this question to expert. You might put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I questioned the witness significantly enough on this issue and this point and that in fact brings me to the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have some additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Professor Skavic, let's start with the experts, some other authors, who could challenge your method and approach to your work. You have mentioned a population study. Does this population study mean that you, in a specific case, in the territory of Croatia and Bosnia, examined this particular population and does that mean that you have arrived at some exact factors which you estimated were the best factors in the identification of the said population? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You did. This was a population study carried out in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Is there anybody more competent anywhere in the world? Is there a better analysis that could be applied to this particular population? Is there any formula better than the one that you have arrived at? Is this the strongest and the best set of figures that could be established?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, there are population studies for different populations. This is the only one that matches our population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Another question with regard to this: If we now took into consideration this expert mentioned by Mr. Stringer, if this expert came with his table to our area, would all of his results be incorrect with regard to the things that you have researched so far?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I would like to put it in a different way. If any expert, including this one, came here and carried out a population study, he would arrive at identical or similar data or factors that we have arrived at, i.e. the factors would not differ significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let's go back to some questions posed by my learned friend, Mr. Stringer. I would like to simplify some things with you. Harmandzic's body identification was based on several factors, some objects, clothes, medical findings. If we look at one factor at a time, let's look at the skeleton first. My learned friend Stringer put it to you that the skeleton belonged to a male, the skeleton indicated the age of some 45 years or so, and some other elements could be seen from the skeleton. If we had nothing but the skeleton and the information that it was a 45 year old female [As interpreted] whose height was 186 centimetres, could we eliminate Nenad Harmandzic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The calculation would not match the living height of the person, which was 196 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now we introduce some other identification elements, a pair of jeans, a lighter, a buckle, a belt buckle and so on and so forth. Is it important for you, when you carry out your identification, is it the family who tells you first what the deceased had on his or her body, or is it important that you first showed them what has been found and then they confirm that it belonged to their next of kin? So what comes first?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this segment of identification in Bosnia. In Croatia, there are the so-called pre-mortem data. Every family, every member of the family, independently fills out a form, mentioning all the important elements, starting with height, weight, personal signs, dental status, ending with the articles of clothing if they are familiar with those. So these are the data which are the so-called pre-mortem data, and they exist before we start the identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: This is very important because Dr. Zujo couldn't tell us, he didn't remember, whether he obtained the information from the son before the post-mortem or later. Another question with regard to the objects found on anybody's body. Is it the same or is there a significant difference if that object, a shoe or an article of clothing, is found on the body, or if that objects are found in the mass grave close to a skeleton? Does it make any difference for you when you approach the post-mortem, if an object was found on a body or if the objects are found somewhere near the skeleton?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I emphasised that in my answers. When we are talking about this group of elements, such as shoes, belts, buckles, lighters and so on and so forth, if those objects are found next to the skeleton, next to the cadaver, then their significance is much less than if the body was found dressed and with those elements on the body. So the elements such as lighters, if they were found in the trousers, in the pockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Based upon your experience, my learned friend Stringer that is shown us some of your findings in which you used the same method. So what you take for granted is what the family tells you; is that correct? Do you take that for granted?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: All this is data that we compare with the data on exhumation. So the data provided by the family before we did the exhumation, a long time ago, sometimes, is compared with the findings of the post-mortem. So some of these -- that information is provided even before we had the body. We obtained the post-mortem information for every person that was found missing in the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you obtained the information from family and you match that information with your other data. What if later on it appears that the data provided by the member of the family is not correct because later on a witness appears who says that he swapped clothes with the deceased? Would that then change your findings, if you subsequently obtained information contrary to the information obtained by the family? Would that alter your findings?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in any case, if new information appears, then one has to determine what the weight of the new information is. Whether the identification was made on the subsequently based data or on some other data, so the situation differs from one case to another, and your approach differs from one case to another, when it comes to the subsequently altered identification data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, we still have another 90 minutes to go, so there is no hurry, because the interpreters have some hard time to catch up with you. Please make a pause after you hear the answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the warning. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: We have a situation here that we have information furnished by the son, and at the same time, we have testimonies by witnesses who have provided us with the description of the clothes that differ from the clothes that were found on the -- during the identification. So if you -- if you had -- if an expert had different information about the clothes, would the expert then be compelled to alter his findings or would he leave it to somebody else to make an estimate?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: In any case, one would need to find out who was it who last saw the deceased, how much time elapsed between the moment the family saw the member of their family alive until the moment when this other person saw him. In a case like this, the post-mortem finding has to be reviewed if it was based on the statement given by the family, as a result of a more recent data which is more relevant for the identification of that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Let's go back to the other identification factors you mentioned, the teeth, you also said that a dentist is a part of your team. I would really be interested in the teeth. You said that you compared the dental status with the dental records. Where do you find the dental records?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: When a body is prepared for identification, and we've done it for years, then all the persons from the immediate family are asked to give pre-mortem information. Then we obtain, through official channels, dental records of all the missing persons. So that we even before we find the body, we already have the records containing data on every person, including dental records, for which we don't even know whether we will need it, but we do have them. Likewise, from every family, we obtain photos. Likewise from all the people who are looking for their next of kin, we obtain blood samples or saliva samples for the DNA analysis so that at this very moment, we have some 2500 processed genomes of the members of the immediate families of all the missing persons, so if at any given point in time, we have any doubts, then based on this available information, we will complete our identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The body of Nenad Harmandzic, who was formerly a member of the MUP, would it be possible to find the dental records of such people in the MUP? Because I believe that MUP has its own dental records for its members. So would that be a customary procedure when you do the identification of such persons, in order to establish who they are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
