utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We object, Your Honour, on the grounds that this is beyond the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We believe so, that, Mr. Par, I think your question is already beyond the scope of the cross-examination. You may rephrase your question or put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Skavic, have you ever carried out identifications of MUP members?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And when you did such identifications, did you ask for the medical records from the family or from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to my learned colleague I really think this is not only beyond the scope of the cross-examination but this is now well beyond the scope of the original expert opinion that Dr. Skavic submitted to the Court and we object on both of those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We agree with you. Mr. Par, skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my learned friend Stringer examined Professor Skavic about his findings. He asked him about the dental status, which is not mentioned in his findings. He said that his analysis was based on the dental status. Then my learned friend Stringer asked him how come that it doesn't transpire from the findings that there was a dentist here? I'm not clear why I am now beyond the scope of the cross-examination if Mr. Stringer has mentioned that in ten of his questions? I'm asking Mr. Skavic about the method in order to see a simple thing, and that is whether there was an omission on the part of Dr. Zujo and Dobraca that -- and that was that they didn't ask for the medical records from the MUP when they were carrying out the identification of a policeman. That is all that my questions are aimed at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that proffer is beyond the scope of the cross, it's beyond the scope of the original expert conclusions that have been given. He's never said that before. And if he's allowed to testify about that now, I would respectfully request an opportunity to cross-examine again on what is a new point but it is a new point, Mr. President, and we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par, we believe that it is a new point of the argument, so I think it's out of the scope. You may skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to abide by your ruling, so I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Professor Skavic, at the beginning of the cross-examination, my learned colleague Stringer faced you with some of your identification findings, trying to prove that your findings based on the same method used by Dr. Zujo and Dobraca, are to be considered reliable and that Dr. Zujo's and Dobraca's findings based on the same method should not be considered reliable. My question is as follows: When you say that Dobraca's and Zujo's finding is unreliable, is it based on the facts that in their identification factors, there is a discrepancy, where in your identification findings there is no discrepancy? Is that the reason why you say that their finding is unreliable?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I've already answered a similar question and I emphasise that in the two cases, two documents presented to me in respect of the identifications carried out at the department of pathology in Zagreb, there were three elements in this it particular case, it was the height, the dental status and the elements furnished by the family and confirmed by the family. Therefore, all the elements are in favour of a positive identification. If any of the important elements were at variance, then the identification could not have been considered positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And finally, Professor Skavic, how could this disputable identification be made indisputable? What about this DNA analysis? Could this method be applied today to the same cadaver? What procedure would that be? What would it consist of?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Since Dr. Dobraca's findings say that the denture is partly preserved and that the bones are preserved, a sample taken from the teeth and from the bones would enable a DNA analysis in order to either confirm or rule out the findings that the body belonged to Harmandzic. So in addition to that, a sample would have to be taken from the blood or the saliva or the next of kin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, professor. I have no further questions. Your Honours, I have completed my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for a break. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judges questions? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Doctor, I have a number of questions to ask you. I find your evidence quite fascinating, especially when we contrast it with the evidence that we've heard previously. Can I ask you, doctor, if you have any comment or inference or conclusion to draw from the length and size of the bones in relation to the possible body build of the person on whom the autopsy was being carried out, pre-mortem?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is not possible to do on the basis of the bones. The best illustration is why is it impossible to give an answer in this way is that, for instance, in a family, you have an individual who is the same height, in the 20s, or 30s, and perhaps weighing so many kilograms less than when that same individual reaches the age of 40 or 50. We cannot say -- we can establish on the basis of bones whether that person had any muscular strength or not, but not much more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Maybe that's what I was trying to ask you. Could you draw any inference from the state of the bones as to whether this person was a strongly built person or a finely built person?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, people of athletic build will have in their also -- system more pronounced places to which individual muscles are connected. So that in a person, in a strongly built person, in an athletically built person, you will see a small knots in places of contact between muscle and bone and that is the only way one can establish whether somebody was strongly built or something else but you cannot draw any other explanation or say anything else about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I take it therefore doctor that you personally can't comment because you didn't see the condition of this cadaver? You're only reporting on reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Doctor, during the break I looked up this word and I couldn't find any meaning that approximated the use of the word in an autopsy. What does dactylography mean? It's not a word that I'm familiar with apart from the root having something to do with fingers. Dactylography.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: It is an identification method, which is based on papillary lines. So dactylography is possible only if you have a fresh cadaver when the fingerprints preserved before are compared with the fingerprints taken after death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That sorts that out. It obviously didn't come into play in this it particular case. I just noticed it from one of your reports. Doctor, can I refer you to the report that was prepared by Dr. -- The original doctor. It wasn't Dr. Zujo, it was Dr. Zujo and his colleague, in relation to the autopsy of the alleged Harmandzic. And I think it was on page 3, where he dealt with the condition of the skull and the teeth.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me something more about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it myself. Give me a moment. It's Dr. Dobraca's report on the autopsy of the body that was subsequently identified as Mr. Harmandzic's body, and it's in relation to -- I think it's on page 3 of the report, in relation -- the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that the expert has Dobraca's report with him, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He does have it, Mr. President. I can refer the Registrar to one of the exhibits that I did not use during the cross, which is marked as Exhibit number 877.1. That's the 94 bis statement of Dr. Zujo, and then the actual report that I think Judge Clark is referring to in the B/C/S language is Exhibit C to that report. So you have Dr. Zujo's report is the first document, and then you have the Dobraca record of expert witness interview in English as Exhibit A to it, and then Exhibit B is the French version, and then Exhibit C is the one that I think the witness would want to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think the document is 00960 something, and does the word "zubi" mean teeth? If it does, then that's the right one. It's witness statement of Dr. Dobraca and it's on page 2. Have you found it, doctor?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I am looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think actually we may be referring to what's marked as Exhibit D to the 94 bis statement, which I know the Registrar has in Zagreb, again Exhibit D to Exhibit 877.1. This is an OTP witness statement of Dr. Dobraca with an interview date of 1 March, 2000. Is that -- Judge Clark, is that the -- because there is the OTP witness statement of Dr. Dobraca and then there is, of course, the actual report of Dr. Dobraca which goes back to 1998, at the time of the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It's described as a witness statement but from reading it appears to be one that wasn't prepared for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [inaudible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm wrong about that, it says, "I'm prepared to come, willing to testify before the ICTY in The Hague should it become necessary." That one. And it's dated -- where is the date? 1st of March, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, Judge Clark. That's his OTP witness statement, and for the Registrar, yeah, the ERN number on the top right-hand corner of the first page would be 00922647.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: What is the Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D attached to Exhibit -- which is a part of Exhibit number 877.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is a procedural matter, and I need to say it. I don't understand, after all this, who is examining the witness? Is it -- is the OTP helping or confusing the witness with these interventions? With regard to a very specific and clear question asked by Judge Clark, the witness will know what this is about and then he'll know the answer or he won't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the Judge could ask any questions, he or she could, and if there is a misunderstanding or refer to any documents, I think both parties will help the Judges to find which document it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm causing the confusion. If Madam Registrar could assist the witness, and I apologise, Witness, if I'm confusing you. There are two reports I'm referring to, one is called a record of expert witness interview and it's Exhibit A of Exhibit P846. And the other one is Exhibit D. That's in English, of the same exhibit, I believe, and it's also -- obviously you'd want to find the reports in your own language because I'm referring specifically to the dental findings.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: If I can tell you what I have before me, this is information where Dr. Zujo says that because of the state that the teeth in the upper jaw are in, both on the right and the left-hand side, it was impossible to use that as an identification method because of numerous fractures. But in the lower jaw, -- but he says that it they were able to establish the state of teeth in the lower jaw, both on the left side and on the right side. And then, when asked, he says that they did not use the teeth for their identification purposes because they would have the dental -- because they had nothing to compare the dental print with. This is the only thing about teeth that I can locate now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We are talking about the same thing, doctor, so if we agree that the report from the autopsy would indicate that there were no teeth in the upper jaw because of two possible -- two possibilities, the bullet which had entered the cheek exited through the mouth, destroying and removing the teeth, or that that had happened but that anyway, the deceased may have worn a prosthesis. Do you accept that that is what has been reported?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: As for the upper jaw, yes, that is what the report says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Would you therefore, doctor, be affected in any way by the evidence which a family member gave that the late Nenad Harmandzic had a partial prosthesis?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: As we have already stated, yes, that is one of the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, doctor, it appears to me that there have been a series of possible identification pointers in this case, quite a number of them. I don't have to enumerate them. But my understanding of your evidence is that you exclude or ignore all those pointers, uniquely on your thesis is that the length of the femur and the humerus do not correspond with the formula for height as described by family members.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I have already spoken about the weight of individual identification elements. From the information about the changes established in the lower jaw, and Dr. Zujo says that in the lower jaw, the right lower jaw, three molars, and on the left-hand side, teeth from the third to the 8th were missing, this is an important identification element. Yet there is no explanation whether they were missing because they had been extracted or broken before, after death, or what. So if we talk about the teeth, this important element of identification was not covered at all. I have already pointed out how important the state of teeth is important, and that is why I said that a dentist must be incorporated in the team to analyse this element in a competent manner. I also said that all the elements that favour the conclusion that the cadaver indeed belongs to Nenad Harmandzic are there, but this particular pointer, and I mean bones, is at variance with them, is dissonant and that is why it requires to be verified by another accurate method.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Doctor, would you accept -- and I'm sure you would -- that there are infinite varieties in the human form and that one can say what one ought to find in general or in principle, in other words a small person usually has small feet and a very tall person usually has large feet but I am sure that you will have found the rare tall person with small feet and vice versa. You wouldn't exclude the person from being tall on the basis that his feet were extraordinarily small, would you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: As for the foot, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. Can I ask you if the calculation of height by long bones is a science or an art?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is a combination of population studies and calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So, doctor, it's not an absolute, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: From my calculations, doctor, in order for the femur of this particular skeleton to accord with the description of the height as given by family members, the femur would have to be 2.1 centimetres taller or longer.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I didn't analyse that but if you have the height of 196 divided by this factor, then we shall have a bone, the length of which would suit such a particular person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: 52.12. So what I'm saying to you, doctor, is you are prepared, as I understand it, to exclude a number of findings which in themselves are probably not of great weight but cumulatively could be, you're prepared to exclude all those on the basis of a femur that is 2.12 centimetres shorter than your formula; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to repeat it once again. I do not exclude any one of these elements. All I do is point out that one of them, which is very important, is at great variance with the information about the height of the late man in lifetime, and therefore calls for the verification by another accurate, reliable method.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: But I think you'd agree with me, doctor, that we are talking in terms of 2.12 centimetres in a skeleton which is almost six years old.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: A skeleton almost six years old, that is its femur, did not change over that time. It couldn't become shorter by 2 centimetres and 12 millimetres. If it was in one piece as the expert says then it would have to be the same length as on the day of death rather than 2 and something centimetres shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor, but if you were measuring a femur at an autopsy and indeed I'm sure you've done it many, many times, do you measure it straight up or in the form in which it lies in a live body? What do scientists do? Do they measure it lying down straight and measure it that way or do they bend it a little bit horizontally as in the photograph of the report that we were shown by Mr. Stringer? He might be kind enough to find it for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Judge Clark, this is Exhibit 956 and the 7th page of that has photographs that show two different ways to measure the length.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: It has to do with the team who opts for a particular method of measurement whether they will do with a bone horizontally or vertically, but the length calculated must always be the same if it was done in the proper way. What we do is that we have a channel, a conduit, with three wooden sides, and one of them is fixed, a fixed wooden plate next to which the bone is put. And the other end is sliding. That is it can be moved. And with this moveable part, we press the bone length wise along the fixed wall, and in that groove we have a fixed scale in millimetres and that is how we measure the bone, always in the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you to speculate, as my last question, but before I ask that, and I think as you're an expert, it's an educated speculation. Normally we wouldn't ask anybody to speculate. It wouldn't be right. But I'm just going to ask you this one thing, which is not speculation. Would you find normally, in an extraordinary coincidence, that a bullet would be found among the skeletal remains of a person who is described as having a bullet in his body when alive? Would you find it an extraordinary coincidence if a bullet should be there, in the absence of it being the actual bullet?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Although it is said that the projectile was next to the cadaver, I would nevertheless consider it very important but not sufficient for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: My final question, doctor, which is asking you for your expert opinion, which, in the absence of your expertise would be speculation but I don't believe it is when you're an expert, if the DNA on somebody in this situation, and we are not talking about Mr. Harmandzic, if the DNA results indicated that the body was the person described, how would you, as a scientist, and as an expert, deal with the variance between the femur length and the given, pre-mortem height?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: Since there was some interference, I'm not quite sure if I heard the question correctly. If I did, my answer would be as follows: The DNA is a reliable method. The only reliable method. And if the result of the DNA were either positive or negative, then no other identification method could affect that result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I put it this way? Suppose you were -- you had a body, the 20th body of those 20 unfortunate Croatian soldiers who were discovered and who were the subject of a report prepared by you and referred to by the Prosecution. You described how 19 were positively identified and one remained unidentified because the description didn't accord to the findings. Just suppose for a moment that that person had a number of indicators of identification, such as age, gender, injuries, teeth -- no, teeth might be too positive, but clothing, clothing, footwear, and suppose his femur was too short for the description given by his family. Suppose the femur were well outside your formula but the DNA came back positively. How would you react to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that none of these identification elements can be confronted or -- with a positive DNA finding, so in this assumed case that you have described, the positive DNA identification would confirm the identity. Everything else is not to be confronted with the DNA analysis and result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And would you not also say, doctor, that that was yet another example of the infinite variety of the human form?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I could absolutely comment on that, but for identification, it would be absolutely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges's questions? Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just one, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, this goes to the last couple of questions that Judge Clark asked you, about situations where you may be confronted with very conclusive DNA evidence which is not consistent with the examination of -- or the information of the cadaver that's in front of you. You said that you read Dr. Zujo's testimony when he came and testified in this case. I want to read you is just a short passage from that testimony and ask you whether you've confronted the same situation in your experience. This is what Dr. Zujo said. In fact it was in response to a question from Judge Clark. This is what Dr. Zujo said: "I work on identification every day. I have such cases that, where you have documents, you find complete documentation on the body, so the parameters are 100 per cent accurate, but that would be drastically different. For instance, I find some cases where they had a metal plate in the femur and I can find that, and yet the height does not agree with the height that I calculated, which means you have a deviation." Now, my question, Dr. Skavic, is just that: Have you encountered situations where you have a very strong identification based on documentation or other information, and yet the height calculation that you would have obtained, based upon measuring the length of the femur, does simply not correspond to the height that you know the cadaver to have been while alive? Have you ever encountered that in your practice?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I already said that in every case, we take samples for DNA analysis, it to prevent such dubious identifications. If there are 100 per cent certain indicators of the identity, then that person can be identified without a DNA analysis, but in this case, this is not the case. This is the case of a number of parameters have not been taken into account or they give a wrong picture. One is the dental status, which hasn't been taken, and the second is the height, which is at variance. So here, based on the existing data, we cannot talk about a positive identification but about a doubt as to the identity of the person. However, that doubt has to either be confirmed or ruled out by a method.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, then, Dr. Skavic, again coming back to the testimony I just read, if the family member, if a family told you that their missing relative had a metal plate attached to his femur while he was alive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this way of posing questions. If the Trial Chamber is allowed to speculate, I do not believe that the same right can be granted to the Prosecution. You cannot proceed by asking Dr. Skavic what would happen if you had been here or there? This Dr. Skavic is taking questions about this case, and this is what he has done. How can the Prosecutor be allowed to enter into a zone that the Judge Clark has just opened slightly? This goes beyond the scope of this expert's testimony. I object to this speculative way of asking questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer. We only heard the part of your question but I believe that there is some speculations in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting, it's just from my point of view this is important evidence and these experts are obviously crucial to the case. I thought that Mr. Stringer asked a question which elicited an answer which was not responsive in total to the question, and then it led Mr. Stringer down a line of questioning to which Mr. Par objected. The problem is that it was an interesting question and I'd like to hear the answer to it from Dr. Skavic because it doesn't involve speculation. I don't know how to roll this back but I know that you asked a question of Dr. Skavic in relation to previous findings. If you can find it and pose it again and see if we could get the answer, I think it's important to hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Dr. Skavic, again, the question is, and I'll try to rephrase it: Aren't there situations where you are presented with conclusive evidence establishing beyond doubt the identity of the cadaver such as, for instance finding a metal plate holding a femur together which the family told to you look for, or documentation found on the family -- on the cadaver with other information, so that really the evidence is conclusive in that respect. Would you still reject the identification even on those grounds or on very solid grounds, simply because it did not fit into your own formula? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I understand your question. Many times we've had situations like this, because that is a very important identification element, and in every such case, either the family or the institution which had carried out the procedure or there are x-rays from the checkup, then these x-rays are compared with the x-ray of the bone found in exhumation. If these two correspond, then the identification is positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that in that situation, a calculation of the height or an assumed height based and your own tables would be secondary to the other information that is before you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: When I started talking about tables and factors, I also mentioned population. These factors and the population studies are carried out on healthy individuals. An deformations due to trauma or due to atypical build are anomalies, deviations from the customary findings, so no population study means anything in such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Just briefly, Professor Skavic, when talking about the exhumations of war victims, does it often happen that bullets are found by these cadavers, that are being exhumed? Is that -- does that happen often or rarely?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the complete situation, with regard to the fact that the biggest number of these people were murdered by fire weapons, very often we come across projectiles, parts of projectiles, parts of explosive devices and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Would it then be rare or common to find bullets which have nothing to do with the death of a particular victim? Have there been cases like that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: There are projectiles which caused the death and there are also projectiles which caused the wounding at the same moment or before that. I can't say for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you have the possibility in such cases to establish whether the projectile has anything to do with that particular body or came to the grave from another source? Do you have the possibility to establish that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP SKAVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that possibility at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you Professor Skavic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, professor, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence. We learned a lot from your expert testimony. We all wish you good luck in your future work. The usher may take you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage are there any documents to tender into evidence? Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would like to propose that this testimony, as a Defence Exhibit, but this has already been admitted as D425. At this moment I'm not aware of the status of this document. On whether it has been admitted conditionally, because it was used in the cross-examination of Dr. Zujo. If that exhibit has not been admitted, I would like to tender that document for admission. Maybe under the same number. And that is D2/25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No objection to its admission, Mr. President. We obviously dispute the findings that are contained in it but we don't object to its being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It has been admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then, Mr. President, on behalf of the Prosecution, there were four exhibits referred to during the cross, Exhibit P113.2, 802.13, 802.14, and P956. And in addition to those four, again just for the record, we would -- we are assuming that the expert report of Dr. Zujo which was submitted under Rule 94 bis is already in evidence but that's what we would tender in respect of Dr. Skavic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We will check it. Any objections, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an objection. We object to the Exhibit P956. We do not object to any of the earlier exhibits, so the findings by Dr. Skavic, P802.13, 802.14, and we do not object to the excerpt from the Croatian medical journal, P113.2. However, we object to the admission of the Exhibit P956, for a simple reason. This is a document that was not suitable for the examination of Dr. Skavic, for the cross-examination, because the document has not been translated. Dr. Skavic could not say anything about the document. He asked for some time in order to read the document, to be able to say something about it. So we cannot accept the admission of a document on which the witness couldn't say anything. The Defence has not received it in time in order to be able to give it to this witness. So we don't find this document admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the other three documents, that is P113.2, P802.13, and P802.14, they are admitted into evidence. As for document P956, this Trial Chamber would like to reserve its right to make a decision at a later stage. After we go through all the transcripts. Yes, it is so decided. Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before we break I had one inquiry to make of the Trial Chamber in respect of the proceedings for tomorrow. I know I asked this earlier but I think there was some confusion whether the Prosecution should be prepared to hear evidence from any of Mr. Martinovic's witnesses tomorrow if we finish with the first witness before the end of the day? We weren't sure whether the Trial Chamber intends to continue then tomorrow after the first witness is done or whether the Trial Chamber intends to recess tomorrow after the first witness and then begin with Mr. Martinovic's witnesses on Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, would you please inform us whether your witness has arrived in The Hague or not? Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I remember well that on the 28th of August, Mr. Stringer asked the same question and you, President, said as follows. We can check with the transcript. Today we will hear Professor Skavic. On the following day, we will hear the witness for Mr. Naletilic, and then on Wednesday, we start with the first witness for Mr. Martinovic. This is what we want to adhere to and this is what we intend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You did not answer my question. My question is whether you know or not whether your witness has arrived in The Hague or not, or when are they expected to arrive here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, late yesterday evening, three witnesses arrived in The Hague, and the first one of them will be ready on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Yes? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask you a question, maybe I have not understood well your orders for the further developments in this trial. I've consulted Mr. Meek. I'm talking about rebuttal and rebrief. You said that it was subject to changes. Have I understood you well or not? If it is not subject to changes, as Mr. Meek understands it, I would like to submit a motion. A complaint, because the way the further course of the trial has been envisaged we cannot agree with that. We have a number of motions that we would like to submit to this Trial Chamber. If this is subject to changes, then, okay, if it is not subject to changes, that will give me the opportunity to rethink what I'm going to do next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the order of the witnesses for this week, tomorrow we will hear the witness in Mr. Naletilic's case and on Wednesday morning, we will hear the witnesses in Mr. Martinovic's case. So is that quite clear? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We may not have understood each other. I'm not talking about this week. I'm talking about the final brief and the rebuttal. I'm clear on the schedule for this month but I'm not clear on the rebuttal and the final brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have to deal with one thing after another because Mr. Seric raised the order issue, we have to deal with the issue first. And then as for the rebuttal and rejoinder procedures, I believe that this Trial Chamber has made a decision on that. And if there are any views, any difficulties that both parties might encounter they may let us know through a motion. We will see what is to be done according to our previous decision. And we have to remind both parties that this case could only run until the end of October. You may find that in the calendar there is no court schedule for this case in November. So having said that, we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
